title: H-1B Visa Cap Reached for FY 2027 Under New Wage-Based Selection System
excerpt: USCIS confirms all 85,000 H-1B visa slots filled in the first selection cycle since the Trump administration replaced the random lottery with a wage-weighted process, as registrations drop nearly 40 percent.
body:
• USCIS announced on July 17 that both the 65,000 regular H-1B cap and the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption have been filled for FY 2027, with no second lottery planned.
  • This marks the first cap season under the new wage-based weighted selection system, which replaced the decades-old random lottery and gives priority to higher-paid, higher-skilled workers.
  • Total registrations dropped 38.5% to roughly 211,600 from nearly 344,000 a year earlier, reflecting the combined deterrent effect of the weighted lottery and a new $100,000 fee for overseas-based petitions.

All 85,000 Slots Filled, No Second Draw

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services confirmed on July 17, 2026, that employers have submitted enough H-1B petitions to exhaust the full fiscal year 2027 allocation of 85,000 visas — 65,000 under the regular cap and 20,000 under the advanced-degree (master's) exemption. The agency said it will not conduct a second lottery this cycle.

Employers whose registrations were selected during the March 2026 lottery had until June 30 to file complete petitions. Approved workers will be eligible to begin employment on October 1, the start of the new federal fiscal year. Unselected registrations will not carry over — those applicants must re-enter the lottery in March 2027 for FY 2028.

The First Test of a Wage-Weighted Lottery

The FY 2027 cycle was the inaugural run of a fundamentally redesigned selection process. Under a final rule that took effect on February 27, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security replaced the traditional random lottery — used for decades — with a wage-based system that ranks applicants by salary level relative to their job category and geographic location.

Higher-paid workers at Level 3 and Level 4 wage tiers now receive priority in the selection pool. The administration has argued that the old random draw was exploited by employers, particularly staffing firms, that flooded the system with lower-paid registrations.

"The existing random selection process of H-1B registrations was exploited and abused by US employers who were primarily seeking to import foreign workers at lower wages than they would pay American workers."

— Matthew Tragesser, USCIS Spokesman

The new system retains the beneficiary-centric model introduced in 2024, under which each worker can be entered into the pool only once regardless of how many employers submit registrations on their behalf. USCIS said this has helped curb duplicate entries and improve program integrity.

Registrations Plummet Nearly 40 Percent

The most striking data point from the FY 2027 cycle is the sharp decline in demand. USCIS received approximately 211,600 unique beneficiary registrations, a 38.5 percent drop from the roughly 344,000 submitted for FY 2026. While USCIS has not yet released final selection rates or detailed cap statistics, the decline points to a chilling effect from two major policy changes working in tandem.

First, the wage-weighted lottery has made it significantly harder for entry-level and mid-career positions to clear the selection threshold. Second, a $100,000 fee — imposed by presidential proclamation effective September 21, 2025 — now applies to new H-1B petitions filed on behalf of workers located outside the United States. Workers already in the U.S., including F-1 students changing status, are generally exempt from the fee.

Immigration attorneys say these combined changes have prompted many smaller and mid-sized employers to rethink their H-1B strategies entirely.

"If the system favors STEM roles, US degrees, or higher-paying jobs, we'll see a clear shift in demand toward certain academic paths, institutions, and employers."

— Husain Tinwala, President, upGrad Rekrut

Indian Professionals Face a Reshaped Landscape

Indian nationals, who secured approximately 207,000 H-1B visas in FY 2024, remain the program's single largest beneficiary group by a wide margin. But the restructured system has introduced new layers of uncertainty for Indian workers at every career stage.

Entry-level workers and recent graduates from U.S. universities — long a core pipeline for Indian talent flowing into American tech companies — now face steeper odds under a system that explicitly rewards higher compensation. Indian-owned IT consulting and staffing firms, which historically submitted large volumes of H-1B registrations for mid-tier positions, are among the most directly affected.

The expanded social-media vetting introduced in late 2025 has compounded the disruption. Immigration attorney Brandon Lai told Spiceworks that mass visa appointment rescheduling "left many Indian H-1B workers stuck abroad for months, and in some cases close to a year, during visa stamping." Some professionals have begun exploring alternative pathways, including STEM OPT extensions, cap-exempt employers at universities and research institutions, and relocation to countries like Canada that have rolled out competing skilled-worker programs.

On the upside, the beneficiary-centric system has improved individual odds for those who do enter the lottery. One immigration firm reported that nearly 80 percent of its H-1B registrations were selected last year, a marked improvement from the old system where multiple-registration gaming by some employers depressed everyone's chances.

Legal Battles and What Comes Next

The overhaul has not gone unchallenged. In October 2025, a coalition of plaintiffs — including unions, health care organizations, schools, and religious groups — filed the first lawsuit challenging the $100,000 fee, arguing it would cripple hiring in underserved sectors. Separate legal challenges are expected to target the wage-based selection process itself, with critics contending that the Immigration and Nationality Act mandates visa issuance in the order petitions are received, not by wage tier.

Business groups have warned that the system will shut out early-career professionals who are precisely the workers most likely to build long-term careers in the United States. Universities, hospitals, and rural school districts say they cannot compete on salary with major tech firms and risk losing access to the visa pipeline altogether.

USCIS has said it will release additional data on the FY 2027 selection cycle in the coming weeks. For now, the roughly 126,000 unselected registrants face a 14-month wait until the March 2027 registration period for FY 2028 — their next chance at an H-1B slot in a system that has been permanently redrawn.
nri_angle: Indian nationals are the largest H-1B beneficiary group, and the shift to wage-weighted selection disproportionately impacts entry-level Indian workers, recent graduates, and IT consulting firms while improved lottery odds benefit those who do qualify.
